body.text: In mid-October, Sengwon (Joe) Cho was told that his company’s work in Ukraine had to stop. Cho is CEO of Newtype Industries, a Seoul-based defense startup that had been testing its AI-enabled artillery software, Barbara, with Ukrainian military units. In an interview, he said a Ukrainian representative overseeing the cooperation told him that an order had come from above to stop all work in this area.

While it is unclear who issued the order or why, Cho is certain that the ongoing rift between South Korea and Ukraine is to blame. “The main reason for ending the cooperation was the diplomatic conflict between South Korea and Ukraine,” he said, referring to the row over Kyiv’s disclosure that it had sent two North Korean POWs to Seoul.

Newtype is one small company, but its case sets a precedent. In August, Newtype was billed as the first Korean defense startup testing in Ukraine, while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed interest in a drone deal with Seoul. Newtype’s experience shows that such ties can quickly evaporate when nothing formal stands behind them.

Newtype’s software, Barbara, addresses targeting and communication – a key weakness of field artillery, according to Cho, a former South Korean field artillery officer. A soldier speaks a report into a smartphone and the voice-focused AI converts the report into a structured message for the fire direction officer. The software can highlight possibly incorrect coordinates or a possible target in a civilian area, but the final decision to fire is made by a human.

Prior to the dispute, Newtype was in regular contact with Ukrainian military representatives and local partners to discuss technical aspects of the trials and to arrange for them to take place. The last such contact was in mid-October, days after Seoul announced the recall of its ambassador. Since then, contact has been completely severed, the company says.

Planned trials, field feedback, and talks about adopting the technology have been canceled or postponed indefinitely. Newtype made that call itself, Cho said, because the basis for cooperation had collapsed. It has also stopped looking for new Ukrainian partners.

Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry declined to comment, saying it does not comment on private initiatives. There is no official confirmation of a link between the stop-work order and the diplomatic dispute. Newtype’s work with Ukrainian units has always been limited by the demands of the battlefield, as units prioritize combat over the testing of products. But Cho rejected the notion that the current situation is simply a military or scheduling issue.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry official said that assistance to Ukraine would be treated separately from the dispute with Kyiv. Some analysts also told the Kyiv Independent in mid-October that the row was unlikely to do lasting damage. However, for a private defense startup such as Newtype, aid is not the main issue. The company’s field trials rely on personal contacts and on the willingness of individual officers to answer messages from the company.

Defense analyst Olena Kryzhanivska told eToday in August that Korean startups testing in Ukraine are isolated cases, with no procurement, joint development, or dedicated channel to support them. That leaves them exposed. Worse, the chill may be spreading: Segye Ilbo reported on October 28, citing diplomatic sources, that Ukraine is considering a review of investment talks with South Korea.

Both sides stand to lose from the end of cooperation. Ukraine loses access to a battlefield tool that its units were testing. South Korean defense firms lose access to a test bed for their products that is very difficult to replicate. North Korea, by contrast, continues to draw on insights from its cooperation with Russia, according to Kryzhanivska.

For now, Newtype has no plans or timeline for returning to Ukraine, though it may reconsider if relations normalize. “Virtually all the partnerships and the local network of contacts our company had built have stopped functioning,” Cho said.
